fatal_errors: The proposed material is CoCrFeMnNi, whereas the target is single-crystal equiatomic FeNiCrMn; adding Co changes the chemical system and its defect energetics.
The intervention reconstructs neither the crystallographic-direction comparison nor the molecular-dynamics temperature and strain-rate matrix.

Changing composition to change lattice distortion cannot isolate lattice distortion or solute drag because stacking-fault energy, elastic constants, chemical short-range order, and dislocation mobility may all change simultaneously.
The cited evidence does not directly demonstrate lattice-distortion-induced solute drag causing enhanced dynamic strain hardening in CoCrFeMnNi.
explanation: The response supplies a testable alternative hypothesis, a nominal control, operating boundaries, measurements, and a falsification rule, so it is not wholly unsupported. However, it does not reconstruct the target mechanism or observations. The target concerns anisotropic yielding in an FeNiCrMn single crystal, thermal softening, yield-strength insensitivity over 10^8–10^10 s^-1, increased dislocation density and flow stress at higher rates, and vacancy-assisted nucleation of Shockley partials producing stacking faults without twinning or bulk phase transformation. None of these distinctive predictions appears in the generated hypothesis. Its comparison is also intrinsically confounded because compositional tuning alters many properties besides lattice distortion. E2 supports high friction stress and low stacking-fault energy only indirectly, not a dynamic solute-drag mechanism; E1 concerns a different refractory alloy and provides little relevant support. Direct measurements of dislocation velocity or mobility, activation parameters, and rate-dependent drag under matched defect energetics would be needed to make the alternative mechanism discriminating.
